name: Jalkunan
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Heath, Jeffrey. 2017. A grammar of Jalkunan (Mande, Burkina Faso). Ann Arbor: University of Michigan / Language Description Heritage Library (MPG PuRe), xiii+420 pp. DOI 10.17617/2.2346932 (CC-BY 3.0).
catalog_locator: Ch. 3 Phonology, sec. 3.1 'Internal phonological structure of stems and words', sec. 3.1.2 'Metrical structure', p. 14; sec. 3.8 'Tones', p. 48; sec. 3.9 'Continuity-marking clause-final M-toned prolongation', p. 65.
catalog_quote: 3.1.2 Metrical structure In the absence of overt stress, metrical (rhythmical) structure in African languages of this zone is most apparent in patterns of vocalic reduction (to schwa or zero). Certain positions in Jalkunan are especially relevant. First, stem-initial CvCv allows Syncope of v1 = i and sometimes of v1 = e when C2 is l. The tone of the syncopated vowel is retained; I show it in (13) as rising tone on the following vowel, but phonetically the L-tone begins on the lateral. (13) bìlí ~ bə̀lí ~ blǐ ‘gave’ bèlé ~ bə̀lé ~ blě ‘passed’ [...] Second, the medial syllable of word-final …CvCvCv can syncopate. This is most apparent in nouns and adjectives when followed by the nominal suffix -ra. [...] There is much variation from one stem to another, and some free variation for individual stems, in my assistant’s speech. [3.8 Tones] There are three tone levels, H[igh], M[id], and L[ow]. Contour tones on single syllables are HL, HM, LH, and MH. Contour tones occur chiefly on word-final syllables, including monosyllabic words, and may reflect Apocope, e.g. /Cv̀Cv́/ → Cv̌C.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Jalkunan is a three-level tone language (H/M/L, lexical and grammatical tone) with no overt word stress; the only metrical (rhythmic) organisation Heath identifies is vowel reduction/syncope in weak positions: the first vowel of stem-initial CvCv (i, sometimes e, before l) and the medial vowel of word-final CvCvCv, i.e. no stress placement rule is given because none is claimed to exist.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress; syncope is optional/variable by stem and speaker (p. 14-15).
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the word/stem; 'overt stress' is denied for the language as a whole in an areal framing ('African languages of this zone'), then applied to Jalkunan positions. Clause-final continuity intonation (terminal prolongation + M tone) treated separately in sec. 3.9.
new_statements.identity_note: Heath 2017 describes Jalkunan as spoken in Blédougou (Blé) and Kinkinkan, Léraba province, Cascades region, Burkina Faso; ISO 639-3 bxl = Glottolog jalk1242 (also known as Blé, Jali/Diali). Single main consultant (Wamara Traoré). Same languoid as the target; no dialect mismatch.

sources.note: Ch. 3 Phonology, sec. 3.1.2 'Metrical structure' (p. 14): no overt stress; metrical structure shows only as vowel reduction/syncope (v1 of stem-initial CvCv when i/e before l; medial vowel of word-final CvCvCv). Sec. 3.8 (p. 48ff): three tone levels H, M, L with contour tones, lexical and grammatical tone, tone sandhi. No other mention of stress/accent placement in the grammar (a full-text search for stress/accent full text: only other 'stress' hits concern an unstressed discourse particle).
